utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gjogaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence will now continue. You'll be asked questions by representatives of some of the accused. I simply have to remind you that the solemn declaration you took at the beginning of your yesterday to tell the truth continues to apply to your evidence today. The next counsel to question you will be on behalf of General Pavkovic, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gjogaj. Mr. Gjogaj, I'm not going to be very long with you. I have just a very few questions. On 16 May 2005, just a bit over a year ago, you gave a statement to the war crimes prosecutor from Belgrade. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you came here to the Tribunal you brought a B/C/S copy of that statement with you and gave it to the Prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about when it was that you first advised someone from the Prosecutor's office about the existence of this statement? When did they first know of it, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day when I reported to the Tribunal's office in Pristina, that's where I -- when I brought it. I was called to meet the Tribunal in Pristina and I brought this statement with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that back on the 16th of May, 2005?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you refer to the one in B/C/S, is that the one you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's in your --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be helpful if I could give him a copy of it. It's been -- it's been put in the -- in the e-court system, but it's not uploaded yet. I don't know why it takes as long as it takes to upload something, but it does. But it was given to them quite some time ago. Anyhow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the P number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, it's a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's 4D21, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's only in B/C/S and English. We don't have an Albanian version of it, but that would be the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you have before you the statement that I understand you brought here when you came. And what I want to know is when the Office of the Prosecutor first became aware of that statement.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean to the OTP of the Tribunal or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, to the OTP of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day we had the preparations, that's when I handed over the statement in B/C/S that I gave in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That statement was taken, though, in Pristina on the premises of The Hague Tribunal, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there someone there from the OTP on that day when you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they were, but I did not recognise them. I was taken in an UNMIK vehicle from my house and straight to the offices of the Tribunal there. I just asked if there was an interpreter into Albanian, and that's all I asked. I had no idea that the statement was taken in Serbian. What I was saying the interpreter was interpreting into Albanian. Now, whether she was an interpreter of The Hague, I don't know that. I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not a very clear answer, is it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not, but I don't think I'm going to get much further with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No one there introduced themselves to you as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor or as an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to me he was a lawyer in Pristina of the Office of the Prosecutor. He said he was from Belgrade and that he was dealing with crimes committed during the war and crimes that had to do with the Tribunal as well. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would have, I take it, been the deputy war crimes prosecutor from Belgrade, whose name is Dragoljub Stankovic; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is his name. I think this is -- what I gave to the Tribunal is the original. I don't see the reason why it should be photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you read Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, when I came here to give a statement I am not that educated; I've only completed five years of school. I don't know how to read B/C/S. I do know the language as a language, but I don't know how to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Mr. Gjogaj, and to remove any uncertainty. During the giving of this statement, you were speaking in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why -- what was the need for the translation into Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just scared that I might make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will -- that question will become clear in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you'll notice at the -- at the beginning of the statement, I think it's probably on page -- it's the page that has 531 at the top of it, K0532531. It indicates that that lawyer from Belgrade, that deputy prosecutor, explained to you what was going to happen, that he talked to you about your duty to tell the truth without omitting anything, and that giving false testimony was a crime, that you were not required to answer any question that would expose you or certain other persons to serious disgrace, significant material damage, or criminal prosecution. That's what the Prosecutor told you at the beginning of that statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And following that advice from the Prosecutor, you then went ahead and gave your statement, which was the truth and from which you omitted nothing. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was working on, of course I stated everything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And what you told that Prosecutor that day was the truth, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And once you completed this statement, then the Prosecutor, if you look at the -- you'll see this on the very -- I think it may be the very last page -- next-to-the-last page. It's the page that ends with the numbers 543. And it says that the state prosecutor reminded you that you had the right to request that the record be translated and read to you, and you said that you wanted that to happen. And as you just told the Judge, you wanted that to happen because you wanted to be certain that it was accurate. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so the record was read and interpreted into Albanian, which it says you understood. And then it says that you said that you had no objection to the contents of the record or to the interpretation because it was accurate and complete. And then you confirmed it with your signature, and we can see your signature on each page of that B/C/S document. And that's all correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this statement basically describes those events in April of 1999, regarding the exhumation of bodies and placing them in a refrigerator truck that you talked about here yesterday. True?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's also true, isn't it, that nowhere in this document, in this statement, which you were told you should tell the truth and not omit anything, did you make any mention of the Yugoslav army or of anyone dressed in the uniform of the Yugoslav army, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes you made no such mention; that's what you're telling me, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday in your testimony here at -- it's at page 56 in the rough transcript, Your Honours, beginning at line 12, you were asked about your boss and how he was dressed at the time he came to order you to go perform these activities. And for the first time ever, as far as I can tell from reading all of your statements, you mentioned that he was dressed in the clothes of the Yugoslav army. Those were your words. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because our boss wearing the clothes of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there some reason that you didn't tell the prosecutor from Belgrade that when you gave this statement and in which you agreed not to omit anything?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't ask me whether they had these clothes or not, otherwise I would have mentioned that my boss was wearing military clothes. They just asked me in general, not in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you do concede, don't you, that the prosecutor told you you should not omit anything?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't ask me if my boss was wearing these clothes or not. My boss was wearing military clothes and when he sent us there, we did what I described in my statement. That's what he worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not challenging that at all. I'm not challenging that you did what was described in your statement. Prior to your testifying here yesterday, did anyone tell you that it might be important if you could somehow bring the army into your testimony and mention an army uniform? Anybody tell you that might be important if you could remember it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your boss was not a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, was he?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our boss was wearing clothes of a soldier; he was wearing army clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know. You told us that. But he wasn't a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, was he? He didn't -- he wasn't a part of any unit, he didn't have a commanding officer that he reported to, he was just wearing a camouflage uniform. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My boss was an ordinary soldier. He was mobilised. He was wearing the army clothes. He didn't have any ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you don't know that he was mobilised; you're just assuming that he was because you saw him in an uniform. But as far as you know, he just put in an old army uniform because many civilians in the area were wearing old army uniforms at the time. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will have just a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gjogaj. My name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law, one of the counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic. Your boss, Buda, we mentioned him a minute ago, for how many years was he your boss with the company, I mean before 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I joined this company, he was there working as a boss already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The firing range we mentioned, and we even saw some photographs of it, this is a large open area, a meadow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question very well. You referred to the firing range?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, the figure range. This is a meadow, an open space, an open area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness inserted an answer, a brief answer saying:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Lukic starts, I would like to have leave to the part and as I do so to ask that 4D21 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's there, along with every other exhibit here in the sense that it's been used and to that extent it's part of the record. So you need have no reservation, no worries, about its admission so far as you need --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know there's some kind of a process that the registry requires to get it in the proper file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We try to avoid using it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your departure, though, just so that I'm left in no doubt is presumably on the basis that you don't anticipate cross-examination of the next witness. There remains a possibility of another witness today. You're aware of that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I have no awareness of that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- well, I don't know what the plans are exactly, but there's a witness, Hamide Fondaj, who I understood arrived last night. Now, I don't know whether that witness is to be led today or not yet, but the witness was on the list for this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, Fondaj is not expected to be led today as she just arrived and proofing is -- I believe is taking place as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, there you have the answer, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gjogaj. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. Dan Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Without mentioning the paragraph number from your statement, I will try to elaborate or clarify something, but should it be necessary we can refer to your statements at any time. In your first statement you mention the exhumation of bodies in Pusto Selo. Is that correct? This is the February 2000 statement.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The procedure of exhumation in Pusto Selo was controlled -- or rather, supervised by an investigative judge and the prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. In your statement dated the 27th of February, 2000, you state: "A guard at the mortuary in Pristina told us that the court asked the police in Prizren to check the bodies." Therefore, is it correct to say that the procedure was supervised by an investigative judge? He may not have been present in the field, but do you have any knowledge that the exhumation was requested officially?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was requested by the court in Pristina. I don't know anything about that. But I know that we took these bodies to the morgue in Prizren and that on several occasions they were taken to Pristina for autopsy and then again returned to the morgue in Prizren. Some of the bodies after that were buried, some still remained there. Just to put it shortly, I was an ordinary worker. I don't know anything about what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the police escort you all the way to the site of the exhumation and while you were engaged in it? This is the exhumation in Pusto Selo that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was with us because in the beginning they cleared the terrain for us not to be a target or something, so they cleared the terrain first. And then afterward they brought us there, after 15 minutes or 30. Then we carried out our part of the work in a hurry and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You carried out the work in the day-time. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The police was securing the site, but they did participate in the actual exhumations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was securing us. We were assisted by other workers from Rahovec, so we, the employees of Hygijena in Prizren and they from Orahovac, worked together and brought then the bodies to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Each corpse was taken out individually. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Each corpse was put in its own plastic bag?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that site the corpses were taken out of individual graves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were normal graves, separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were photographs taken of each corpse. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Each corpse, after having been exhumed, was marked, a tag was put on both the body and the bag. Did you see that as well?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we were carrying these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the bodies were first taken to Prizren to the hospital and its mortuary so that Dr. Hidajet cause examine the bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were taken to Prizren, that's true, but as for Hidajet, whether he was appointed to examine them or not, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that all the bodies were taken for autopsy to Pristina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, all of the bodies were again re-buried in individual graves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we conclude, therefore, as far as you know that the exhumation process in Pusto Selo was undertaken publicly and in keeping with regulations?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness would not be aware what the regulations would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll rephrase. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your view, was this exhumation carried out publicly? Was anything being hidden or concealed?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were just brought there, and when we went there I didn't see anyone in that village. We were ordered to perform our work in three hours, to take out the bodies. It was a rainy day. We were very tired. We couldn't even stand on our feet. It took us five hours to take the bodies out, and then we brought them to Prizren. I didn't see anyone in that village except for my colleagues and the police that was protecting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were they protecting you from, these policemen?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were protecting us from, but they were in charge. They were there to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about exhumations and the firing range and the garbage dump. Is it correct that this exhumation was carried out in a manner which was opposite in all its aspects when compared to the exhumation in Pusto Selo? If you wish, I can actually deal with it question by question. Were you escorted by the police over here, too, from your home to the place where you were supposed to carry out this exhumation?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this other place, Buda came, my boss. He collected me from my house with his car. When we went on the site, the excavators were already there, ready for their work. They were just waiting for us, the workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So from your home to the place where your took your equipment and then from there to the site where the exhumation was to be carried out, you were not escorted by the police, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our boss, who was with us, was wearing an army uniform and probably they had agreed between themselves because we were in his car and on the site itself we were there and the police was around us to secure us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The work at the firing range was carried out during the night, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that the policemen took part in digging up the bodies over there as well, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb police was working with another excavator while we, the workers of Hygijena, we were working with another excavator. They had one refrigerator truck and one excavator and we had one refrigerator truck and one excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What am I trying to say? This particular spot, as opposed to the other one in Pusto Selo, at this particular spot at the firing range, the police in your view took part in digging up the bodies, too - that is what you said - and loading the bodies on to the refrigerator truck, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was working as we did, in the other hole with the other excavator. So the police was doing the same work. They were digging up the bodies and then they were putting them in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this site, the bodies had not been buried individually and they were not being taken out individually, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No pictures were taken on this site after the bodies had been exhumed, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The bodies were not marked during this exhumation either, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not take these bodies to the hospital in Pristina or to the morgue -- to the hospital in Prizren or the morgue in Pristina, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We loaded these bodies on the refrigerator trucks. The trucks remained there. We got on the Volkswagen make car of my boss and we were taken back to our company in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now conclude that the exhumation procedure at the firing range and at the garbage dump was completely different from the one carried out in Pusto Selo?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In Pusto Selo the bodies were buried individually, and in this other location the bodies were in two different holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Right now I don't have an updated transcript from yesterday, but yesterday in response to a question put by my colleague Ms. Carter in line 67 -- or rather, page 67, line 19, you described where this grave was at the firing range. You mentioned that it's below the police station. Are you trying to say that the police station is close to the military artillery firing range or was that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me? Well, first the Lubishte police station comes and then there is a meadow and you take the road that leads to the firing range.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, how far away is this firing range from the police station?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A hundred metres? A kilometre? Five kilometres? Roughly. You don't have to give us an exact number.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how far it is, but it is close, maybe 200 or 300 metres. But I cannot be accurate in this because I don't know. I never measured the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this a police station or a police check-point? I think that in your statement to the investigating judge from Belgrade you refer to a police check-point.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sort of a station. Now, whether it was a police station or a check-point, I don't know, but the police was there, the police responsible for Lubishte and the surrounding area. It served as a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could hold on a minute, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Carter, the witness in the statement refers to an investigator going with him to these locations. Is the investigator to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The investigator's not on our witness list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems pretty basic that if a witness points something out to an investigator, no doubt he would take a photograph, that all of this would be tied together and it would make it much easier than the exercise we're going through, but that hasn't been done?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, to the extent that I am aware, this witness is not on our witness list at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We'll struggle through. On you go, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, Mr. Gjogaj, my learned friend Ms. Carter asked you -- or rather, she put something to you, namely, that at the firing range you and people from your company were in a hole, in a pit when you were getting the corpses out. Were you in there when you were taking out the corpses or was it the excavator that was getting the bodies out, whereas you were waiting by the truck to put them on to the truck?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to explain things very simply here. I was not the only one that loaded the bodies on the truck. We were four of us. It was the excavator that dug the bodies out, and then we loaded the bodies on to the truck. I think this is very simple. I don't know what else to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you didn't go down into the pit, you didn't, right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're on the subject of the firing range, did you recognise any of the policemen over there at the firing range? Did you see someone there that you knew?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not recognise anyone. It was night-time, it was raining, and the police were around us to protect us, so that nobody would come and harass us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about Dr. Hidajet in the Prizren hospital. Do you know what his ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hidajet, do you know what he is by ethnicity? Is he a Serb, an Albanian, a Gorani?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to have something placed on e-court. 6D74, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, I'm going to ask you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Carter --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- about these camouflage patterns, whether you'll be able to recognise some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the use of any exhibits by the Defence with this witness. All three exhibits that I believe are going to be proposed to be used by the Defence were all known or knowable by them prior to this witness ever taking the stand. They were not submitted into e-court until after this process had already begun today. We had no notice of them yesterday before we came into court, and only once the session began did they ever get released on to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a serious objection? I mean, you are seriously taking this point, in view of the Prosecution's behaviour in relation to these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I do believe that there is a differentiation. The items that are being used by the Defence at this point in time are -- were known or knowable by the Defence prior to this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why should they use them if you haven't got your act together and have not put your exhibits into the system? Why should they use them?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, when we receive items they go into the system as quickly as possible. The items that are issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you just throw things in willy-nilly without thought. Why should anybody who's thinking about his case put these items in when you have been unable to find the colour copies of the photographs? Why should they help you to prosecute their clients? Tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, again, the position of the Prosecution is simply that colours, uniforms, all of these things were at issue prior to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but if you can't get your act together and put photographs in, why should the Defence provide you with what you can't do yourself? Tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence had these items --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you answer my question? Should the Defence be helping you to make your case against their clients?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, that is the job of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. And if you can't get the exhibits together, why should they put stuff in that might assist the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm not certain what answer that you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I take the view that your objection is -- well, let me consult with my colleagues first before I express a personal view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We repel the objection. You may use the documents, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gjogaj, if you look at this photograph with different camouflage uniform patterns, can it be of assistance to you? Can you recognise the camouflage pattern that you saw at the firing range? If you can. If you cannot recognise it, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I have been in the army. I have done my military service. I have not seen such kind of uniforms in the army. I know what SNB is, I know what Vojna Policija is. I did not see these colours at the time I completed my military service. I was not an inspector of military clothing. What I know is the army is the army and the police is the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see in the system 6D73?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do that, Mr. Gjogaj, have you looked carefully at all of these? Because you'll see that there are 37 of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see them but I cannot tell the colours. I told the people of the Tribunal what the colours were. I have not seen these colours ever in my life. As I told you, I know what the police are and the army are, but I cannot all the -- know all the colours that army wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we see 6D73 on e-court now, please? [In English] Can you zoom it in, please, a bit so it's bigger? That would be fine, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gjogaj, what about this photograph, do you see a pattern that would remind you of the pattern that you saw at the firing range on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Which one is it? Can you describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain this to you -- multi-coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see on e-court P2317 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before you move on, do you wish this one photoed -- photographed and given an IC number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the Court would like it done --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- if you don't mind. So we'll give this an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC43, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll need to note that that is a Court exhibit. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I asked for another document to be put on e-court now, P2317, page 16. [In English] I'm afraid it's not that one. We found something else on the page number 16. We should move five pages up, so it would be 46 at the end. The whole number is K0075546. It's the third attachment, I was told. In English version, the third attachment, page number 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which statement is it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gjogaj, underneath these photographs, can you see your signature? Down there, underneath the photographs, it says "Gjogaj," right? Is that your signature or --

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this page we see four black and white photographs. You put three X's there in circles. What was it that you were marking on these photographs?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked about this occasion. I couldn't explain everything that was done in Prizren. I explained here. What I was asked to do I did, and I said that police came and asked us to work. Maybe I make the mistake here. I am a living person, a human being, people make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this photograph, could you tell us what it was that you marked actually. What were you asked to mark?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they asked me: What kind of uniform? Before I came here to the Tribunal, somebody had -- came and asked me at home: What uniforms were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So at the firing range you saw all of these uniforms? Were they police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, the camouflage patterns that are at issue and the markings that are at issue are actually a part of the first statement which involves Pusto Selo, so I believe it's a misstatement and a mischaracterisation to say that he was describing what was occurring at the firing range using these demarcations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are these referred to in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are in the English version, they would be the -- basically the tenth and eleventh page of the first statement that was given on February 27th of the year 2000 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This attachment, Your Honour, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just a moment until I have -- one at a time. We'll begin to understand it. My statement only goes to page 7 I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the first page on the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Lukic, while I deal with this. Now, Ms. Carter, you said it's the tenth or the eleventh page. I think I only have -- I have got seven pages. Now, I want to know where in the narrative the witness says something about these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not a part of the narrative, as best I can tell, but as to where it comes in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know where I've got it, but what I want to know is how it fits into the statement. Is it just a hanging document without any link to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It does not appear that there is a demarcation such as with the no photographs, that the investigator apparently went through this document with him, had him make demarcations, but unfortunately did not put within the narrative of the statement what those X's meant to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you understand these X's meant?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that he was identifying -- testimony has not been elicited by this attorney in regards to Pusto Selo. It is my understanding that there are two lines, first police, then military on the outlying areas, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, just stop. This is too complicated. Why is it part of your 92 bis package if you're not relying on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- we are relying on the de -- the colour copy showing which uniforms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know you're relying on the colour copy, but that -- the witness has used it in a completely different way from this. What is the purpose of this document being with the package?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That in regards to the Pusto Selo he was identifying both military and police uniforms at the time, is my understanding of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But at the moment -- at the moment there's no evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, somehow we got these patterns attached to the statement from the 24th of June, 2000, and even in the e-court these both statements are attached and at the end we have these pictures. So even from the e-court it's not clear whether it comes with the first or with the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no date against the signature, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can do two things here. We can either request a full explanation of the situation from the Prosecution, which you would get in writing, or you can cross-examine the witness about it and see how far you can get the matter clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I think that Ms. Carter is on her legs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, you simply look to the Bates stamps. The ERN number's on the top. If you look at them in order, it very clearly indicates -- with the original numbers that you can see a strike-out on them and even the numbers above that numerically these documents come with the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can see that there might be a basis for suggesting that, but how does that help us in identifying the date at which the witness actually paid attention to this document? All that that establishes is that that document was available when these numbers were applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You can at minimum know that those documents are close in time to the first statement, as there is a clear break in numerical order between the first statement and the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All -- all I'm suggesting to you is that that doesn't help us to determine whether they were both dealt with at the same time, because when they are put into your numbering system is not necessarily the date on which the statements were taken, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, they are not immediately put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, what do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can ask one more question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, do you remember when it was that you were asked to identify and mark these photographs? Was it in February or June of 2000?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I forget. It's been a long time. It's been four or five years from then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gjogaj. We have no further questions for you, and I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I have no further questions of the witness. However, I do want to point out to the Court apparently it assists if I actually read statements with my eyes open. On paragraph -- the fifth paragraph down of the English specifically denotes that he is putting X's on camouflage patterns, and that's involving the Pusto Selo statement. And I do apologise for the confusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the statement of the 27th of February?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And that's involving the Pusto Selo, not the firing range or the garbage dump.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say it's the fifth paragraph? One, two, three -- oh, yeah. So Mr. Lukic was right in assuming it was connected to that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Mr. Lukic has been implying that that was involving the firing range. That was where my objection came in is that I believed he was identifying in relation to the Pusto Selo -- it was my understanding from Mr. Lukic's argument he was trying to say that these uniforms were being identified at the firing range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the problem -- the remaining problem is that that refers to putting on X on the top of the two uniforms that are recognised, and there are three X's. You don't have any insight into that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, I'm sorry that there's been some confusion about one or two matters in your evidence, but I think you've given us as much help as you can; thank you for that. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who speaks in relation to the next witness? Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Shefqet Zogaj under Rule 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The paragraphs are paragraph 72(d), 75(d), and 77. Actually, he refers to events which took place in Suva Reka and Belanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're on the topic of the paragraphs in the indictment that this witness is to give evidence on, I wanted to raise one point. Not having had the decision on K82 available to me, I don't know precisely the bases of the Court's findings in regards to that witness, but I note that this witness statement for this witness discusses a number of killings and attacks upon villages that are not referenced in the indictment. And so I just want to bring that to the Court's attention. Again, without having the decision I don't know whether I -- I guess I ought to object, but I don't know how strenuously that should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are -- just hold the witness outside for the moment. These are villages adjacent to villages which are mentioned in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. My main concern was with the -- there's a number of killings addressed at pages 3 and 7 of the first statement which are not enumerated in the -- in the indictment at all. The -- my reading of the indictment shows that the only killing that is alleged is with respect to the incident involving the Berisha household.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I'm looking at page 3, which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At page 3 it's the third -- there's the list of four individuals in the middle of the page, Ramadan Sukaj, Hafiz Shala, Osman Elshani, and Albert last name unknown. And then on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've not found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's page 3, ERN number 00755395 it looks like. Do you have his -- that's the first statement from 1999, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, what's your position on this? It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- said that the killings are confined to the Berisha family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The killings referred to in the statement, which we purpose to impart with the evidence, if one looks at pages 2, 3, to 5 are part of a narrative of the deportation from Suva Reka and the surrounding villages, part of a narrative of killings, crimes against Albanians which led to 80.000 people being gathered in the fields, in the village of Belanica in particular, and thereafter deported. So this is part of the Prosecution's case, a narrative of killings, crimes against Albanians in Suva Reka municipality leading to the deportation of the people from Suva Reka, from that municipality. If you look at paragraph 72(d) in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 72(d), D as in David, (i) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the killings there referred to are of male persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We consider that the evidence is, on the face of it, admissible on the basis indicated by Mr. Stamp. There's -- there is some force in what Mr. Ivetic submits because where there are events involving deportation which result in murders of people identified, then we would normally have expected to see some reference to these in the schedules. But there is an adequate averment in 72(d) certainly to lead the evidence that's referred to in page 3 on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At page 3, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The position in relation to page 7 may be different. But there comes a point when it is unrealistic to try and divide up a witness's statement. So what the Trial Chamber will do is ensure that in the end of the day regard is not had to evidence which would fall outwith the ambit of the decision we've made, viewed in the spirit of which that decision was made in relation to Witness K82, otherwise we'll spend most of our time in legal argument. But you can rest assured that if something appears to us to fall outwith the terms of this indictment read broadly as we ought to read it but also having regard to what notice it gives to the Defence, then we will exclude that evidence ultimately when we come to deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can proceed, Mr. Stamp, with the witness on the basis of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry. We'll break now and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00 and commence the evidence then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, you -- you should not need any documents of your own. We should have all the documents here. So just please pay no attention to these documents unless someone asks you to do so. It's not appropriate for you to be reading from anything other than the documents that will be placed in front of you. We already have been before us a written transcript of the evidence you gave when you were here on a previous occasion, and we also have copies of statements that you've given. That's the thickness of the bundle of material we already have about evidence you can give the Tribunal, we've read it, so we know what you can say about many things. You're going to be asked questions to either explain some of it further or to clarify things, and you'll be asked questions to challenge it. The important thing is: We don't go through all this again in detail. The important thing is to concentrate on the questions you're asked and to deal with the particular point that arises in each question, because we want your answer to the particular issues that counsel ask you about. So please try to concentrate on the individual points that are raised in the questions, and that will give us the maximum amount of information to enable us to reach the right decision. The first counsel to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zogaj. Please spell your name --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Please state your name and spell your surname.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: My name is Shefqet Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand that you were born in the village of Belanica in Kosovo, in Suva Reka municipality in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I also take it that you are a journalist?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall on the 26th of April, 1999, you gave a statement to offices of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you gave another statement to the OTP on the 18th of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these statements were in relation to events that occurred in your municipality in March and April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 3rd of February, 2002, and the 5th of February, 2002, you also gave declarations acknowledging the truth of the contents of those two statements?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed you made one correction in respect to the statement of the 26th of April, 1999, which --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour -- it's in the English record in e-court. I understand there was some difficulty in getting it on the B/C/S record in e-court. So I'll just take him through it in viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph -- or I should say at page 3 of the first statement, the English statement, English version it is written here that Zoran Lazic was the head of the municipality of Suva Reka. I believe when you gave your declaration on the 3rd of February, 2002, you made a correction and said that in fact he was the chief or the main criminal in the municipality of Suva Reka, in your view, not that he was the head of the municipality. Do you remember making that correction?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, that is in which paragraph -- is it the page numbered 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The page numbered 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the paragraph is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph, first paragraph beginning on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Subsequent to your giving this declaration in 2002, 24th of April, 2002, you also attended here and gave evidence in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. That is correct as well?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the statement of the 26th of April, 1999, with the 92 bis declaration is P2322. That of 18th of June, 2001, also with the 92 bis declaration is P2323. And the transcript is P2324; that is a transcript from the previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these are all now part of the record in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, I'd like to focus primarily on the events of the 1st of April, 1999. But by way of background, I'd just like you to show us on a map where your town is, your village of Belanica is in relation to the municipality -- the other places in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P615 or could it be placed on e-court, please? Page 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom it in a bit because I can't see clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we zoom out a bit now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see it clearly now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or could we have one -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see there towards the left centre of the map the main town in the municipality, the town of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Suhareke here. Then you go towards Duhla, then to Bllace, Temeqin and Bellanice. It's on the seventh kilometre from Duhla to Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your village of Belanica, I would like you to identify exactly where it is on the map first and then put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said by the 1st of April or the 31st of March, 1999, and I'm here referring to the first full paragraph that starts on -- or the first paragraph that starts on page 4 of the English version, and I think the first paragraph that starts on page 4 of the B/C/S version that about -- you said: "On the 31st of March, 1999, about 80.000 people had gathered in the three villages of Belanica," which you just showed us, "Guncat, and Lladroviq." Do you see firstly Guncat on that map?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the other one is Lladroviq.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see both Guncat and Lladroviq?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: It's not Llandroviq, it's the village Lladroviq.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have just circled Lladroviq or is that Guncat?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No, you cannot see it here on this map. It's a little bit higher. If you could lower the map a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we lower it without destroying the markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask the usher if he could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... same map a little lower and we can do the markings very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we can abandon this one and bring it slightly lower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you do it in such a way that we also see Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not here now on this map. It was okay before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you take it up so we see Malisevo at the top of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a little lower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, the other way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now -- now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just put circling around those three towns you just spoke of.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Three villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I think you told us in your statements and also in the Milosevic case that these 80.000 people gathered there by the 31st of March were refugees coming in from the surrounding villages over the previous few days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at about that time, my understanding is that there was an offensive of Serb forces in the area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understood you to say in the Milosevic case as well as in your statement that many of the people gathered, the 80.000 people gathered, to escape the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also told us in your statement that as the Serbian forces attacked or advanced, many civilians were killed. And you named some of them at page 3 of your statement that you knew of, including Ramadan Sukaj, Hafiz Shala, Osman Elshani, and one Albert, whose last name you do not know. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, these people were killed in the town of Suhareke on the 25th and 26th of March, 1999. All these killings were committed by Milorad Nisavic. His nickname was Miska. There was one person who escaped, Sejdi Bytyqi, a history professor from the village of Semetishte.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's indicated in your statement that you got -- in your village and in the surrounding areas that you got this information from people who were coming in that people were being killed. Now, is the fear caused by the information that these people, some of whom you know were being killed by the Serb forces, one of the reasons why people were escaping and gathering in the area of your village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Bellanice was a little quieter until the 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to that --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on that day or prior to the 1st of April, 1999, were there KLA elements or forces in Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The KLA stayed in Bellanice until the 28th of March of 1999. On that day, seeing that from Malisheve and Lladroviq and Nishor, the Serbian police forces were coming from those directions. They left the village and the Albanian population and went to the mountains of Llapusha.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a small intervention for the transcript. Page 39, line 21, I think that this name is out of context. I'm not sure that the witness actually mentioned the name. I don't know how it got into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did mention Sejdi Bytyqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that he was the history teacher who escaped killings in Suva Reka and came and told you about the killings in Suva Reka of civilians?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, Sejdi Bytyqi. Sejdi Bytyqi was one of the witnesses who escaped the execution. And for four or five hours he stayed in the sewage of the Suhareke town in order to be safe, while on the night of the 25th and the 26th of March went to Peqan and Semetishte and then to Bellanice. When he arrived at Bellanice, I met him and everything, I told you earlier about the killings I learned from him, Sejdi Bytyqi, the history teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think my friend is right, it's out of place on that line, but he did mention him earlier in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's at line 14 that the name should go. There's a reference to the name and there's a marcation for the last name. So I think it was just put on the wrong line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it may just be updating the transcript, Mr. Visnjic, but there you have it all in context now. So we can continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's keep focussed on the 1st of April for the time being, Mr. Zogaj. After the KLA left Belanica on the 28th, did they return or pass through Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The night when the military and police forces led by the paramilitaries, the Serb paramilitaries, came from the direction of Bllace, Nishor, Semetishte, Duhla -- sorry, Malisheve, that's what I meant, the KLA was not able to defend its points anymore. So they were forced to leave the trenches. So on the 31st of March to the 1st of April up to 8.00 in the morning, they were there. But after that, no KLA soldier remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to get the sequence correct. The KLA had been in the village up to the 28th of March, and as the Serb military -- and they left on the 28th of March. But as the Serb military advanced --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting my learned friend, but I think that it's quite clear in the transcript what the witness had said, and now this is a leading question and is leading the witness to another answer. The witness said up to the 31st of March -- or rather, the 1st of April they were in the village until the 1st of April quite clearly, the 1st of April, 8.00 in the morning. And now the witness is being led to answer otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be quiet for the moment until we deal with this. Yeah, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not leading the witness to answer otherwise. I'm leading the witness to clarify what he meant when they were there on the 1st of April when he said earlier that they had left on the 28th of March. There's an explanation for that which I think both of us know which the Court should know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And nevertheless I think it's probably correct to say that that's a leading question and that you should deal with this in more open questions. So rephrase that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said earlier that they had left the village on the 28th of March, and you also said later that on the 1st of March they were at the village --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I agree. I think you've got to deal with this with open questions and ask the witness about the sequence of the KLA departing from the village, and then we'll get it clear that way from his recollection rather than from you putting words into his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The KLA left the village on the 28th of March. Do you know about their movements in respect to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we don't know at the moment if that is accurate, because we have a number of dates on which it has already been said that the KLA were in the village beyond the 28th of March. So to say it in broad terms, as you have done, they left on the 28th of March, is putting words in the witness's mouth. I'm beginning to wonder now if you'll get any valuable answers because three times you've asked the same leading question. Do you want me to do it for you or are you going to ask it by -- are you going to ask open questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm putting to the witness what he said. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, what were the movements of the KLA in respect to Belanica on the 28th of March and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 28th of March I said in the beginning -- maybe I was not clear. On the 28th of March the KLA, which was stationed at the village in the old school, primary school of the village, which in fact was shelled later by the Serb forces. At that day they left the village, while members of the KLA who were in their points in Bllace, Semetishte, Peqan, Dragobil, Malisheve and elsewhere came during the night of the 31st of March and 1st of April and went towards quieter villages in the mountains of Llapusha. So there's no doubt about this. You are asking me: Why did they leave on the 28th and why were they still there on the 1st of April? I explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you understand it, Mr. Stamp, I don't. So you should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After the KLA who were based in the school on the 28th departed Belanica, you said that KLA members from the points of Blace and some other areas went to Belanica. Did they remain there or did they pass through Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I said earlier, they passed through Bellanice to go towards Llapusha, to the mountains there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they passed through Belanica on what date?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: It was the night of the 31st of March and 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So to sum up, the KLA that were posted in Belanica departed on the 28th, on the night of the 31st and the morning of the 1st of April other KLA passed through the village. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I will make it clear once again because I don't think it's clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do. Are you saying that that's an inaccurate summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it's clear to the Prosecutor what I said. What I said was the following, that on the 28th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop again, stop again. It doesn't matter whether it's clear to the Prosecutor or not; it's to be clear to the Court. And what the Prosecutor has just said to you is: "What I understand you to have said." Now, are you telling us that that is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Then let us start all over again, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mean what I put to you earlier was correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, members of the KLA that were in fighting positions, they passed through Bellanice in order to get to more quieter villages in the mountains of Llapusha, and I don't know what is not clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now by what time in the day of the 1st of April had they left Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Early in the morning, before 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've -- I mean, that's a -- I find that a misleading question. I didn't realise they were in Belanica on the 1st of April. I thought they were passing through it, but now we have the concept that they are leaving it on the 1st of April. I mean is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By that I mean they passed through and left. I want to know when the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that by 11.00 there were in excess of 30.000 people gathered in the fields at Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Which date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 1st of April. Sorry, I should have put that there.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 1st of April in Bellanice there were around 80.000 inhabitants, 80.000 people from the surrounding villages who were sheltering there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your statement you actually say that on the 28th of March there were 30.000 people in the village of Belanica. Now Mr. Stamp is asking you if that was the position on the 1st of April, but your statement also said -- your statement also says that this increased to 80.000 on the 31st. So he seems to be trying to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- clarify something that may be inaccurate in your statement. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want to get the evidence from him because there might be an issue around the numbers. So may I just ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But where in the statement does he say that by 11.00 there were 30.000 people in the fields of Belanica?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which is what you put to him, that at 11.00 on the 1st of April there were 30.000 people gathered in the fields. Now, show me where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said earlier on that by the 28th of March, 1999, there were about 30.000 people in the village of Belanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He goes on to say that other people were joining them, and then he reaches now to the 1st of April. That is why I put to him that in excess of 30.000, since on the 28th of March there were 30.000 and people were joining them between the 28th and 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I have to say, Mr. Stamp, it's not a very helpful way of trying to advance matters. The statement's perfectly clear and we're getting into oral evidence that's simply confusing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, you said -- or you agreed with me that on the 1st of April, 1999, there were people -- there were in excess of 30.000 people gathered in the fields at Belanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, because on the 1st of April there were around 80.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
