utterances.text: Stop. Why do you want to get back to this figure of 30.000 on the 1st of April, when the statement says 80.000. I mean, I know that 80.000 is in excess of 30.000, but not in the mind of the witness, and one can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said in his statement this: "On the 31st of March, thousands of people from the village of -- villages of," and he names the villages, "... gathered in Belanica." And before that he had said 30.000. He goes on to say: "This increased to 80.000, the number of people who had concentrated in the three villages of Guncat, Lladroviq, and Belanica." So you are saying that he is saying in his statement that 80.000 are gathered in Belanica. I am reading his statement that he said that 80.000 people were gathered in Belanica, Guncat, and Lladroviq. I just want him to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure there must be a particular reason for identifying how many were in the individual three villages, Mr. Stamp, and if there is, then please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- of the people who were gathered in Belanica and the other two villages we mentioned, were there any KLA members at 11.00 on the 1st of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I want to point out here that only in Bellanice there were around 80.000 people, not including Guncat and Lladroviq. If we include those villages, then this number would mount to above 100.000 people. I don't know why is this confusion about Guncat, Lladroviq, and Bellanice. Only in Bellanice there were around 80.000 people on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the 80.000 people in Belanica on the 1st of April, were there KLA members among them at 11.00 or so?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your statement that when the Serbian forces entered the village around 60 men went out with white flags to meet them, and they were seized by the Serbian forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Around 60 men, elderly persons mainly, they went out with a white flag to surrender themselves because there was no other way out for them, while these Serbian military and police forces, following the orders from the above, they beat them up. And immediately after this, after the beatings, they began to expel the population. I want to make something else clear here, something that you didn't mention. The Serbian police and military forces entered the village by shelling from different artillery equipment, like tanks, machine-guns, and other equipment. They didn't enter the village quietly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, I've told you already that we already have this information, and the questions that are being asked are to clarify points, apparently, although one has to wonder whether that's a successful exercise. But we don't need you to go over again what's actually written down here; it's here in our minds already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When the Serbian forces entered the village, you said in your statement that they were burning houses as they entered the village, and then they started to expel the population. Was there any resistance from the people who had gathered? Did anybody fire at the Serbian forces as they entered the village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No, nobody fired at them, not a single person. The Serbs were the ones who fired at the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now you said that the Serb forces that entered the village were composed of the police, the military, and paramilitaries. Can you describe how you are able to distinguish and identify these various elements.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did the police, let's start with them, the police wear? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They had blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The soldiers had green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They had black uniforms and had scarfs around their necks. They had beards. Some of them had long hair, some had shaven heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did these three elements or these three groups act separately or did they act together in formation when they entered the town?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They acted together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned that among the formations that entered the town there were military vehicles. I'd like to show you some photographs of military vehicles now. Could you tell me if you can identify those that entered the town. But first I'd like to clear the map. Could that be given a --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC44, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could 13 -- P1325 be placed on the ELMO? Is this page 2? Could you move to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say whether or not the vehicles you see here were vehicles that were used in the operation in Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many of them?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The one here under number 5, it belonged to the Serbian police. The other under number 6 is of the Serbian army. Number 8 is of the Serbian army. Same goes for number 7. I would like to point out that on the 1st of April in Bellanice not only that they entered by tanks, but they entered using excavators and trucks in order to be able to loot the village and the civilians that had gathered there and afterwards to expel them to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, excavators should be replaced with bulldozers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that the population were expelled and forced to leave in a convoy towards Albania by these Serb forces that you have mentioned. To be more precise, you said they were guided out in two directions. How were the population expelled and guided out of the village.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to mention here that as soon as they entered, the Serbian police, paramilitary, and military forces in Bellanice, they shattered shelling. And as a result of the shelling, two people who were sheltering there from the village of Reti, Nazlie and Drite Kryezliu, mother and daughter, they were killed. A number of people sheltering in Bellanice were beaten and looted and killed. Among those who were captured was myself, two policemen, both of them wearing masks. They took us out of the car and took us to the basement of my house in order to execute me. They were asking for money, and because of the money I managed to survive. They closed the door and told us to stay inside. After they left, I opened the door, left that place, and again went to my car. And in my car they tortured me and they fired at me. And you can still find the traces of this. After I entered the car, another two policemen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop there. We have all this in very considerable detail --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- much more than you've said already. We know exactly what happened to you. The Prosecutor's question wasn't concerned with you alone; it was concerned with all the people who were there. And that's our concern, that we cover the interests of everyone. Now, could you listen again to his question and please try to answer the question that he's going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say, as you've said previously, that these people, the 80.000 people, were expelled from Belanica and were guided out in two directions, explain what you mean in respect to these 80.000 people leaving Belanica in those circumstances. How were they guided out by these Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In order to be able to explain this, I have to go into details because they, as soon as they entered the village, in a savage way they began to beat up the people regardless of their age, regardless of their gender. They were beating up everybody. They were stealing things from them, they were cursing them, offending them on a nationalist basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop there. In case I've misunderstood the position. Are you not trying to find out directions that people were sent and these matters that we need to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because we already have the details of the violence. But we need to know, you think, more about where people went and how they were directed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in particular ways. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said the people were guided out and directed in two directions. Could you tell me which two directions the people were forced out to go to?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The first direction was Malisheve and then to Rahovec, Zazev [phoen], Prizren, and then finally to the Albanian-Albanian [as interpreted] border. The second direction was Temeqin, Bllace, Duhla, Suhareke, Prizren, and Morina. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And which direction did you go?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I went in the direction of Duhla, Suhareke, and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you return from Albania eventually?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I returned from Albania when the war ended, on the 21st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you returned, what was the condition of your village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Bellanice was burnt down, 70 per cent of the village was burnt down. The vehicles that had remained there, that had been stopped there by the Serbian police, military, and paramilitary forces, they were also burned. We have pictures of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From what you've said, Mr. Zogaj, can I take it that both groups went through Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As you said you have pictures of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness brought along with him yesterday some pictures which we managed to scan quickly and disclose them to the Defence and load them on e-court. I would like to show him just a few of the many photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are photographs of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Photographs of the -- of his house that was damaged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When he returned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When he returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we establish when these photographs were taken, first of all? When were they taken, Mr. Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These photographs were taken on the 21st and 22nd of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said you returned on the 22nd, so I think -- can we take it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 21st. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just trying to verify that in fact we have received the documents. It looks like they are now on e-court, but obviously if we did receive them, we received them last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what they are, though, does it really cause any difficulty for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not now that I found out what they are. I stood before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who took these photographs; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P2345, photograph 1 of that set? Could we rotate it clockwise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is shown there?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This is my house. It's burnt. It was burnt by the Serbian police, military, and paramilitaries during the war after the 1st of April. You can see an evidence of the Serb barbarism here, because they couldn't even stand to have our houses in our own land.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the other houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Same meaning that they were also burnt?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Burnt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About what proportion of the houses in the village were burnt and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we also have a look at paragraph 3 -- or page 3 of this set?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the basement of the house where we had our valuables hidden. This is the basement of the house of my uncle where we had hidden our valuables, but this basement was burnt as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us in your statement that people who you knew, and you also named them in your statement, were killed by the Serbian forces in Belanica as you were driven out and while you were on your way to Albania. You also indicated that your relatives, Shaban Zogaj, Sali Zogaj, Elmi Zogaj, and Sami Zogaj were also taken away by Serb forces while they were on their way to Albania and not seen since, and that was up to the time you have testified in the Milosevic case. Do you know if they have been found since that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I would like to point out that Shaban Zogaj, a teacher of geography in our village, was kidnapped in Ostrozub village, and he is still a missing person; while Sali Hamet Zogaj and Elmi Zogaj, when we returned from Albania, we learned that they were found killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand that --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They were found in the cemetery of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at photo number 4 -- or page number 4 of this photo set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you say was the full name of Sali? What's his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Sali Zogaj. This should be his name, and this is not his picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, before we -- forget the picture for the moment. We have a note of a name Sali Hamet Zogaj. Is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Sali Hamet Zogaj. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Hamet but Hamit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The photograph you see in front of you, what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This depicts the killings, the barbarism, the Serb genocide over the Albanian civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't help us. I think Mr. Stamp wants to know more detail about the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Sami Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was he found?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In the cemetery in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you took these photographs. What date did you take this photograph; do you remember? Or can you approximate?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I can't remember. It might be on the back of the photograph, if you have a look, or maybe in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to page 5 of that set? That's the back of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you make these writings on the photograph and does it --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And does it help you to -- help you in respect to the date when you took it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In this note, I cannot see the date of the photograph. This date here shows the date when Sami was taken away, was kidnapped in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to show you three photographs quickly and could you just tell me who they are?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to photograph 6 in that batch?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Can I just make one clarification here or an explanation? Even -- I wanted to explain something about the former photograph as well -- or if you could put all four photographs on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just identify the photographs and then you can clarify what it is you need to clarify. There are a couple others. Who is this?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This is why I wanted all four photographs to be on the -- on the screen, because it's been a long time that I haven't seen these photographs and that would help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why does this matter when these persons are not the subject of murder charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These persons -- these persons were killed in the circumstances which according to his -- to his narrative, these were the circumstances in which they were deported from Kosovo to Albania and they were expelled. The entire environment of terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the relevance. We've dealt with that already. But why do we need to go through an identification process if there's no charge of murder in relation to these individuals. We don't have to make findings about their killings, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not specifically in respect to entering a verdict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the fact of these killings in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it looks like you're going to have to put all four on the screen somehow or other on the screen to deal with the questions that you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You wrote on the back of each photograph the names of the persons who are depicted in the photograph. Could we move to the next page and therefore you could tell us who that person is. Who is that person that was shown?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Elmi Jashar Zogaj, kidnapped on the 1st of April, and he was found killed after we returned from Albania in the cemetery in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to paragraph 8, please, or page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just have a look at the photograph and then we could move to the back of the photograph, which is page 9.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This is Sali Hamit Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case we could move to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say who that is or do you need to look at the back?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, he's Skender Morina from the village of Samadrexha, but we can have a look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This is a picture --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Not Samadrexha but Samodraxha, because they are different. Samadrexha, S-a-m-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This picture shows what in it, the one before you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This picture was taken on the 28th of March when there were about 30.000 people in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what does it show us?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Among these people -- of course these people were people who were expelled from the villages where there was fighting to come to villages where it was a quieter situation, in Bellanice, for example. There were wound wounded people from the Banje village. For example, Velima Begaj [phoen] was heavily wounded and she died in Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is she in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She is not in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, listen to the question. You're being asked: What does the photograph show us? You're an intelligent man. You must be able to understand the questions that are asked of you. Please. So please tell us what's in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see here the people coming from other villages, people on tractors, cars, and also horses and carts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what that photograph shows us, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The people on the left of the photograph, what are they doing? Are they just concealing a clear view of the various vehicles that they were travelling in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see here a white car. The ones the plastic coverings are trailers, tractors with trailers, and the people kept their bare essentials, you know, like food and clothes. This is a Lada make car. And then after -- behind the Lada you can see the tractor, a red tractor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp, the last person who was named from a photograph, do we see that name at all anywhere in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, that person is not in the statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said earlier -- and I'm closing now, Your Honour. You said earlier that one Niskovic, according to the information you had, was responsible for the killings in Suva Reka on and after the 25th of March. Could you repeat the name, please?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Milorad Nisavic. He had the nickname Miska, and he also was known by the name of Milorad Miskovic. That's why he had this nickname Miska. He was known, notorious in the Suhareke area as a killer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was his, if any, role or function officially? Did he have a particular post that he was employed to?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: He was head of the police in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know which section of the police?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know which department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. In respect to the events leading to the expulsion of these 80.000 people from your village and your community, you also I take it gave an interview and related the events to persons from the organisation Human Rights Watch while you were in Albania. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, going back to Milorad Miskovic, at the same point in your statement you refer to someone by the name Zhika?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was also a policeman in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that his surname or his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew him as "Zhika." I don't know whether it was his name or surname, but he was known in the villages around us because he was part of a police patrol that went to these villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know what level he was in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 1st of April -- or better to say, before the war started, the municipality of Suhareke -- he was a policeman in Suhareke. He patrolled the streets in Suhareke and the surrounding villages, especially in Duhla, Bllace, and Bellanice. The people knew him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was an ordinary police officer? He wasn't a commander or a superior officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say. I don't know whether he was superior officer because sometimes these police officers, if they committed a crime, sometimes they were promoted. So I don't know, but I can say that they took part in crimes -- he took part in crimes and he had the regular police uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without a mask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the position is that we would like time to review the recently disclosed materials, which I'm not even sure if we have received them all yet, but we've had notice of them and received parts of them. So we would ask that the witness be released for now and asked to return when we've had an opportunity to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The suggestion yesterday was 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the Prosecutor can tell us whether we've received all the materials. I think there were three books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp -- or Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness brought three books in with him, one of which related only to Dubrava prison, which we did not take. He authored one book, which we have provided the Albanian version of, and he authored a second loose-leaf book, and I'm not certain of the status of that. I am certain that neither of those books have been translated into either B/C/S or English, and I don't have a time on how long it's going to take to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you intending to have them translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is: We don't know. I think it depends on CLSS's availability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure about this, Mr. O'Sullivan, that the case should grow arms and legs just because witnesses happen to have written books and bring them along to court with them. I appreciate the indication that was given yesterday, and that will be adhered to, but it was perhaps precipitate without knowing anything really about the contents and bearing in mind that the Prosecution are not referring to these documents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just been advised that both books have been provided in Albanian; the other is on the same CD along with the photographs in the Defence box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the indication given was probably precipitate and but for the fact that Mr. Ackerman has gone, I think -- I for one would be inclined to insist on the cross-examination taking place just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, what access do you have to someone who can alert you to the contents of Albanian documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe anyone on any team has an Albanian speaker. It would be a question of locating someone, and I don't -- we haven't at this point -- I don't believe anyone has ever done that. So I can't answer that question right now. But when I rose a moment ago, I was speaking on my understanding of what you said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I accept that. I'm not -- but I'm reflecting now that it perhaps was a precipitate statement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We would say, however, that what this witness wrote in his books may indeed be relevant to what he has testified to, his credibility, our Defence cases. I would ask for the opportunity to look at that, realising that these books are in a language that none of us can even look through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, though, in future it may be that when something like this comes up, the cross-examination should, generally speaking, proceed and -- on the understanding that it may emerge that the witness has to come back, whereas -- and then at least there's a prospect that we will not have wasted time and money. On this occasion, obviously, we have agreed to you having the opportunity to consider these documents so that you could conduct -- be sure that you're conducting a cross-examination that was an integrated one. However, this -- these documents don't fall into any category of material that would oblige the Trial Chamber to give you time before commencing cross-examination. They're not statements in the sense of Rule 66, for example. And therefore, we may take a different view on a future occasion. Do you think there might be value in asking the witness to stay in The Hague, at least until next week, to see if in fact a review of these documents is possible in the course of the next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm hearing lots of moaning and groaning, so I think the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, even if the books are to be translated, next week is the week we have court from 9.00 to 6.00 every day, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wasn't so much thinking of translation. I was wondering if you would identify someone who could read them on your behalf and tell you if there was any material that you ought to be paying attention to. The Trial Chamber doesn't take the view that just because a witness has written at length that every page of that has to be translated into the language of the Tribunal and the language of the accused before any progress can be made. Anyway -- Grant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, the two books that have been referred to by Mr. Scully just now, do they deal with the events that we've been discussing today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One of them is "Blood Traces." It speaks of the events, but in a more elaborate way that -- than we spoke about it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other book is a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of? Transcript of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the same book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's only one book then, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one book. This is a transcript. Just a moment. When the prison of Dubrava was mentioned, that's the second book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, leave that aside. We are not concerned with the prison at Dubrava. We are, in this trial, concerned with other events. And I think I understand you are saying that the loose-leaf document was a -- the original manuscript of the book that then becomes a book called "Blood Traces"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there we have. We've halved your work already, gentlemen, ladies. However, we did give an indication which we will adhere to, but that means that we have to determine a date at which the witness returns. And probably the most convenient date would be the 9th of October. Now, is that suitable or do you insist on a longer period? Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I dare speak on behalf of all, but if we get a translation of this book we've just established that there's just this one relevant book, we would stand ready on the 9th. However, if we do not receive the translation, my proposal is if it's not too far away, as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, that it be the first day after the winter recess. By then we'll have the translation and everything. This is a just a proposal, but if we get the translation of the book by the 9th, it's no problem, we'll hear him on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a brave attempt on your part, but a translation of a document like this is -- seems to us an extravagance in the circumstances of this case. The -- this is a document that somehow or other should be read for you so that you can identify particularly the parts that need to be translated. Translation is a very time-consuming, difficult exercise. Only a few pages a day can be done by a translator who is doing something officially for court purposes. So we have to be realistic with these things. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to clarify one matter, and I'm sorry I may have missed it in the colloquy that we've just gone through. But as I read the supplemental statement, there was a book written by Mr. Zogaj entitled "Evidence presented to the ICTY," which, according to the supplemental information sheet, contains information about the KLA, including their role in protecting the Albanian villages. Now, I may have missed in the colloquy here, but I'm not sure that that was specifically addressed to Mr. Zogaj, and my question would be: Is he in possession of that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zogaj, is that part of the book called "Blood Traces"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is part of the book "Blood Traces."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the reason I'm suggesting a fairly early date is that we would prefer to hear the whole of a witness's evidence without too much of an interruption. However, I suspect that the 9th of October would not be a date that would be easily confirmed. So I think what we should do is hear from parties on the 9th of October what the state of play is with this book and when would be convenient for the witness to be cross-examined. But please bear in mind the need to try to hear the witness as soon as possible so that we get a fair picture from both sides of what's being said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so we'll hear what the position is on the 9th, with a view to having the evidence on the 23rd of October. Now, Mr. Zogaj, the problem that's arisen is that the book "Blood Traces" was not known to the Defence until you came here and to enable them to prepare fully for cross-examination of you, they've asked for time to read it. And it's not in a language that they're familiar with, so there's a problem over arranging for some form of translation. So we cannot complete your evidence at this stage. We have to conclude for the moment. I'm -- yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness knows whether his book exists in a second language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to this day, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. So the problem is we'll have to end there, interrupt your evidence, and you'll need to resume it but at a later date. So you'll need to come back to The Hague. You'll have to go home and return here. The provisional date is the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll discuss it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, it won't be the 23rd. That's a day in which we will not be sitting. So it would be the 25th of October. 25th of October you should meanwhile keep available. Now, if there is further discussion that -- to suit the parties, then the Trial Chamber will be alerted, and you'll be told of any change that's made in that arrangement. Meanwhile, and this is very important in your case, you must not discuss your evidence in the case with anyone. Now, that means the evidence you've given already and the evidence you might yet give in the case. Now, with most people, that's quite an easy rule to comply with, but you being a journalist will naturally, no doubt, be keen to discuss all sorts of events with people at every opportunity. I'm afraid that between now and the completion of your evidence, you will have to avoid discussing these subjects which may be part of your evidence with anyone at all because you are in the middle of your evidence, you're bound by an oath to tell the whole truth, and you're bound by practice of this Tribunal not to have any discussion with anyone at all about what may be your evidence in the case and what has been your evidence. Now, do you understand all of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to add something here, that this notebook here, I have notes here which will belong to another book that will be the continuation of "Blood Traces," and these are all pages that have not been made public. And I would like you to take this notebook, and if you could translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No thank you, Mr. Zogaj. That's not an appropriate way for us to proceed. We are dealing with events which occurred seven years ago, and we really have to bring some finality to the consideration of these events within a reasonable time. It is not appropriate for this dispute to be driven on endlessly by the provision of material at random in a disorganised way. Now, that's not your fault in any respect, but you must understand that these proceedings have got to be brought to a close within a reasonable time. And if witnesses continue to come along with pages and pages of additional material, it will never come to a conclusion. If the Prosecution haven't managed to put together their case by now, then heaven help us. So I'm sorry, but it's not for us to take these papers from you and to explore them further. So please bear in mind what I've said to you, and someone from the Victims and Witnesses Section will make arranges for your return here in due course. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do I take it, Mr. Stamp, that that concludes the available evidence for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have a list showing ten witnesses scheduled for next week. It's likely that in the course of this afternoon the Trial Chamber will issue a Scheduling Order to try and give guidance on how these witnesses will be fitted in to the week. If there are any particular problems, therefore, about the timing of any of them, you should alert Mr. Dawson to that as soon as the Bench rises. We'll adjourn now and resume at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.30 p.m.,
